---
id: cpp-stable-compaction
title: Stable Compaction and Move Zeroes
difficulty: Easy
order: 2
tags: arrays, two pointers, in-place, read/write pointer
time_limit: 1
---
## Statement
Two in-place operations, both with the **read/write pointer** technique:

```cpp
void move_zeroes(std::vector<int>& a);
    // move every 0 to the end, keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements
int remove_value(std::vector<int>& a, int val);
    // remove every occurrence of val; the first R positions must hold the kept elements in
    // their original order; return R (the rest of the array may hold anything)
```

Both must run in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. Don't call `erase` inside a loop, because that is O(n²).

**Input:** cases until the end of input: `zeroes n` followed by `n` numbers, or `remove n val` followed by `n` numbers. n ≤ 10⁶. The driver prints the result (the first R elements for `remove`), truncated to 20 elements, plus a checksum.

## Starter
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

void move_zeroes(vector<int>& a) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i)
        if (a[i] == 0) { a.erase(a.begin() + i); a.push_back(0); }   // buggy AND O(n^2)
}
int remove_value(vector<int>& a, int val) { return (int)a.size(); }
```

## Driver
```cpp
static void show(const vector<int>& a, size_t r) {
    unsigned long long h = 1469598103934665603ULL;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < r; ++i) h = (h ^ (unsigned)a[i]) * 1099511628211ULL;
    cout << r << ':';
    for (size_t i = 0; i < min<size_t>(r, 20); ++i) cout << ' ' << a[i];
    cout << " | " << h << '\n';
}
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    string cmd; size_t n;
    while (cin >> cmd >> n) {
        int val = 0;
        if (cmd == "remove") cin >> val;
        vector<int> a(n);
        for (auto& x : a) cin >> x;
        if (cmd == "zeroes") { move_zeroes(a); show(a, a.size()); }
        else { int r = remove_value(a, val); show(a, r); }
    }
}
```

## Hints
- Use two indices: `read` scans every element, and `write` is where the next element you keep should go.
- Copy `a[read]` to `a[write]` only when you keep it. Why can `write` never overtake `read`?
- For move-zeroes, after the pass, fill positions `write..n-1` with zeros.

## Solution
`read` visits every element once. `write` is where the next **kept** element goes. Because `write ≤ read` at all times, a kept element is never overwritten before it has been read. Kept elements are copied in the order they're met, so their relative order is preserved: the compaction is *stable*.

The starter shows the classic bug. After `erase(i)` the next element slides into position `i`, but the loop still increments `i`, so consecutive zeros are skipped. On top of that, every erase is O(n).

`std::remove_if` implements exactly this algorithm. Follow it with `erase(new_end, end())` to actually shrink the vector (the erase-remove idiom).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

void move_zeroes(vector<int>& a) {
    size_t write = 0;
    for (size_t read = 0; read < a.size(); ++read)
        if (a[read] != 0) a[write++] = a[read];      // keep non-zeros, in order
    while (write < a.size()) a[write++] = 0;          // zeros fill the tail
}

int remove_value(vector<int>& a, int val) {
    size_t write = 0;
    for (size_t read = 0; read < a.size(); ++read)
        if (a[read] != val) a[write++] = a[read];
    return (int)write;
}
```
